stem: A telemetry broker stores events on six 7200rpm SATA drives in a RAID-5 array. According to the Kafka design documentation, how do linear writes compare with random writes on that array?
key: Over 6000 times faster, 600MB/sec against 100kB/sec
distractors: About 6 times faster, at 600MB/sec for linear writes against 100MB/sec for random writes
About 60 times faster, at 600MB/sec for linear writes against 10MB/sec for random writes
About 600 times faster, at 600MB/sec for linear writes against 1MB/sec for random writes
explanation: Linear writes run at about 600MB/sec and random writes at about 100kB/sec, a difference of over 6000X. About 6 times is wrong, because the documentation gives about 600MB/sec for linear and about 100kB/sec for random writes. About 60 times is wrong, because the documentation reports a difference of over 6000X. About 600 times is wrong, because the documentation reports a difference of over 6000X.
extract: the performance of linear writes on a JBOD configuration with six 7200rpm SATA RAID-5 array is about 600MB/sec but the performance of random writes is only about 100kB/sec–a difference of over 6000X

stem: A telemetry service appends millions of events per minute to Kafka. According to the Kafka design documentation, what happens to each message the broker receives?
key: It goes to a persistent filesystem log at once, without necessarily being flushed
distractors: It stays in an in-process cache in the broker that remains warm across restarts
It stays on the JVM heap of the broker, where garbage collection cost stays flat as data grows
It is buffered in memory first, because disks are always far slower than the network
explanation: All data is immediately written to a persistent log on the filesystem without necessarily flushing to disk. An in-process cache that stays warm is wrong, because the pagecache stays warm after a restart whereas an in-process cache must be rebuilt. Heap storage with flat GC cost is wrong, because Java garbage collection becomes increasingly fiddly and slow as the in-heap data increases. Disks always being far slower is wrong, because a properly designed disk structure can often be as fast as the network.
extract: All data is immediately written to a persistent log on the filesystem without necessarily flushing to disk.

stem: Kafka serves telemetry consumers from the page cache and uses `sendfile` on a plain-text listener. According to the Kafka design documentation, how does `sendfile` change the path of data from file to socket?
key: The OS sends it from the pagecache to the network directly
distractors: Data still takes four copies and two system calls on every fetch
`sendfile` still applies when SSL is enabled on the listener of the broker
Consumers that are caught up still cause constant reads on the disks
explanation: Using `sendfile`, the OS sends the data from the pagecache to the network directly, so only the final copy to the NIC buffer is needed. Four copies and two system calls is wrong, because that is the common data path that `sendfile` replaces. `sendfile` with SSL is wrong, because `sendfile` is not used when SSL is enabled. Constant disk reads is wrong, because with consumers mostly caught up there is no read activity on the disks as data is served from cache.
extract: Using sendfile, this re-copying is avoided by allowing the OS to send the data from pagecache to the network directly. So in this optimized path, only the final copy to the NIC buffer is needed.

stem: A Kafka producer compresses batches of telemetry events before sending them to the broker. Which set of compression protocols does Kafka support, according to the Kafka design documentation?
key: `GZIP`, `Snappy`, `LZ4` and `ZStandard`
distractors: `GZIP` only
`GZIP` and `Snappy` only
`LZ4` and `ZStandard` only
explanation: Kafka supports `GZIP`, `Snappy`, `LZ4` and `ZStandard` compression protocols. `GZIP` only is wrong, because Kafka supports `GZIP`, `Snappy`, `LZ4` and `ZStandard`. `GZIP` and `Snappy` only is wrong, because Kafka also supports `LZ4` and `ZStandard`. `LZ4` and `ZStandard` only is wrong, because Kafka also supports `GZIP` and `Snappy`.
extract: Kafka supports GZIP, Snappy, LZ4 and ZStandard compression protocols.

stem: A telemetry producer sets the user id as the record key for every event it sends to a Kafka topic with several partitions. Where does Kafka send all events of a given user?
key: To the same partition
distractors: To partitions chosen in round robin for each record
To every partition of the topic
To a random partition chosen for each record
explanation: If the key chosen was a user id then all data for a given user would be sent to the same partition. Round robin is wrong, because with a user id as key all data for a given user is sent to the same partition. Every partition is wrong, because all data for a given user goes to the same partition. A random partition is wrong, because the key is hashed to a partition so a given user always lands on the same one.
extract: on a Kafka cluster where the consumers are mostly caught up you will see no read activity on the disks whatsoever as they will be serving data entirely from cache.

stem: A Flink job aggregates telemetry streams and takes checkpoints. According to the Flink documentation, which operators perform stream alignment during a checkpoint?
key: Joins and operators after a shuffle
distractors: Only operators with multiple predecessors, which are the join operators
Only the sink operators of the job
Every operator of the job, including `map()` and `filter()` operators
explanation: Alignment happens only for operators with multiple predecessors (joins) as well as operators with multiple senders (after a repartitioning or shuffle). Only joins is wrong, because alignment also happens for operators with multiple senders after a repartitioning or shuffle. Only sinks is wrong, because alignment happens for operators with multiple predecessors and operators with multiple senders. Every operator is wrong, because alignment happens only for operators with multiple predecessors or multiple senders.

stem: A shared Kafka cluster gives each unique client group a fixed quota configured by the cluster. On which basis is that quota defined, according to the Kafka design documentation?
key: Per broker
distractors: Per topic, summed over all brokers
Per partition of each topic
Once for the whole cluster, shared by all brokers
explanation: Each unique client group receives a fixed quota as configured by the cluster, defined on a per-broker basis. A per-topic quota is wrong, because the quota is defined on a per-broker basis. A per-partition quota is wrong, because the quota is defined on a per-broker basis. A single cluster-wide quota is wrong, because the quota is defined on a per-broker basis.
extract: By default, each unique client group receives a fixed quota as configured by the cluster. This quota is defined on a per-broker basis.

stem: According to the Kafka design documentation, once poor disk access patterns have been eliminated, a telemetry system of this type has two common causes of inefficiency. Which are they?
key: Small I/O operations and byte copying
distractors: Too many large sequential writes and slow compression of batches
Garbage collection pauses and too few partitions per topic
Too many consumers and excessive replication between brokers
explanation: The two common causes are too many small I/O operations and excessive byte copying. Large sequential writes and slow compression are wrong, because the two causes are small I/O operations and byte copying. Garbage collection pauses and too few partitions are wrong, because the two causes are small I/O operations and byte copying. Too many consumers and excessive replication are wrong, because the two causes are small I/O operations and byte copying.
extract: Once poor disk access patterns have been eliminated, there are two common causes of inefficiency in this type of system: too many small I/O operations, and excessive byte copying.

stem: A telemetry store replicates each item on N=5 nodes and requires W=3 nodes for a successful write. According to the Dynamo paper, what is the smallest read quorum R that yields a quorum-like system?
explanation: Setting R and W such that R + W > N yields a quorum-like system, so with W of 3 and N of 5 the smallest R is 3. R of 2 is wrong, because R + W of 5 is not greater than N of 5, so the system is not quorum-like. R of 1 is wrong, because R + W of 4 is not greater than N of 5, so the system is not quorum-like. R of 4 is wrong as the smallest value, because R of 3 already gives R + W above N, which is enough.

stem: A telemetry pipeline sends events to Kafka, and the Kafka protocol groups messages together. According to the Kafka design documentation, around which abstraction is the protocol built?
key: A message set grouping messages
distractors: A single-message request that the broker never combines
A byte stream with no message boundaries
A key-value record that is always compressed alone
explanation: The Kafka protocol is built around a message set abstraction that naturally groups messages together. A single-message request is wrong, because the protocol is built around a message set abstraction that groups messages together. A byte stream with no boundaries is wrong, because the protocol is built around a message set abstraction. A record compressed alone is wrong, because efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together rather than each message individually.
extract: our protocol is built around a “message set” abstraction that naturally groups messages together.

stem: A broker sends log data to a consumer socket on the common data path, without `sendfile`. According to the Kafka design documentation, how many copies and system calls does that path take?
key: Four copies and two system calls
distractors: Two copies and one system call
Three copies and three system calls
Six copies and four system calls
explanation: The common data path for transfer of data from file to socket has four copies and two system calls. Two copies and one system call is wrong, because the common path has four copies and two system calls. Three copies and three system calls is wrong, because the common path has four copies and two system calls. Six copies and four system calls is wrong, because the common path has four copies and two system calls.
extract: there are four copies and two system calls

stem: A producer compresses telemetry events before sending them to Kafka. According to the Kafka design documentation, what does efficient compression require?
key: Compressing multiple messages together
distractors: Compressing each message individually
Compressing only the message keys
Compressing only at the broker after the write
explanation: Efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together rather than compressing each message individually. Individual compression is wrong, because efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together rather than each message individually. Key-only compression is wrong, because efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together. Broker-side compression after the write is wrong, because efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together.
extract: Efficient compression requires compressing multiple messages together rather than compressing each message individually.

stem: A telemetry pipeline stores vehicle readings in Elasticsearch. According to the Elasticsearch documentation, what do metrics consist of?
key: Data point and timestamp pairs identified by dimension fields
distractors: Log lines and traces kept in a logs data stream
Posting lists of document IDs for each term
Relevance scores from term frequency and document length
explanation: Metrics consist of data point-timestamp pairs, identified by dimension fields, that can be used in aggregation queries. Logs and traces are wrong, because logs or traces use a logs data stream or a regular data stream, not metrics. Posting lists are wrong, because a posting list is the part of an inverted index that lists document IDs for a term. Relevance scores are wrong, because BM25 calculates those from term frequency, document frequency and document length.

stem: A telemetry index in Elasticsearch has 5 primary shards and 1 replica per shard. According to the Elasticsearch documentation, to how many primary shards does each document belong?
key: One primary shard
distractors: Every primary shard of the index
All shards, including the replica shards
Two primary shards, for redundancy
explanation: Each document in an index belongs to one primary shard. Every primary shard is wrong, because each shard holds only a subset of the documents in the index. All shards is wrong, because a replica shard is a copy of a primary shard, not a second home of the document. Two primary shards is wrong, because each document belongs to one primary shard.

stem: A Flink job runs in at-least-once checkpointing mode. According to the Flink documentation, which dataflows still give exactly-once guarantees in that mode?
key: Dataflows with only embarrassingly parallel operations such as `map()` and `filter()`
distractors: Dataflows that contain joins of several input streams
Dataflows that repartition streams with a shuffle
Every dataflow, whatever its operators
explanation: Dataflows with only embarrassingly parallel streaming operations (`map()`, `flatMap()`, `filter()`) give exactly once guarantees even in at least once mode. Dataflows with joins are wrong, because only dataflows with just embarrassingly parallel operations give exactly once in at-least-once mode. Dataflows with a shuffle are wrong, because only dataflows with just embarrassingly parallel operations give exactly once in this mode. Every dataflow is wrong, because only dataflows with just embarrassingly parallel operations give exactly once in this mode.

stem: A producer sends Kafka a compressed batch of 500 telemetry records, and the batch header states 500 records. According to the Kafka design documentation, why does the broker decompress that batch?
key: To validate it, for example the record count against the batch header
distractors: To store the records uncompressed so that consumers read them without decompressing
To decompress it on behalf of the consumer, which cannot decompress data itself
To split it into single records that the broker appends to its log one at a time
explanation: The broker decompresses the batch in order to validate it, for example that the number of records matches what the batch header states. Storing the records uncompressed is wrong, because the batch is written to disk in compressed form. Decompressing for the consumer is wrong, because the consumer decompresses any compressed data that it receives. Appending single records one at a time is wrong, because the server appends chunks of messages to its log in one go.
extract: The broker decompresses the batch in order to validate it.

stem: A Flink job aggregates vehicle telemetry with checkpointing enabled and needs consistently super low latencies of a few milliseconds for all records. According to the Flink documentation, what does Flink offer for that requirement?
key: A switch to skip the stream alignment during a checkpoint
distractors: A switch to postpone the checkpoint snapshots until the job is idle
A switch to align every operator, including operators with a single predecessor
A switch to lose records on restore instead of replaying them
explanation: For applications that require consistently super low latencies, Flink has a switch to skip the stream alignment during a checkpoint. Postponing the snapshots is wrong, because checkpoint snapshots are still drawn as soon as an operator has seen the checkpoint barrier from each input. Aligning every operator is wrong, because alignment happens only for operators with multiple predecessors or multiple senders. Losing records on restore is wrong, because with alignment skipped the records occur as duplicates and are replayed after the restore.

stem: Analysts query per-minute metrics of 400,000 vehicles, and the pipeline adds those metrics to Elasticsearch. According to the Elasticsearch documentation, when should a team choose a time series data stream (TSDS) for its metrics?
key: When it typically adds metrics data in near real-time and in `@timestamp` order
distractors: When it mostly stores timestamped logs or traces rather than metrics
When it runs the data in a Vector Database project rather than an Elasticsearch project
When its metrics carry only a timestamp and no dimension fields at all
explanation: The documentation says to choose a TSDS if you typically add metrics data to Elasticsearch in near real-time and in `@timestamp` order. Logs or traces is wrong, because for other timestamped data such as logs or traces it recommends a logs data stream or a regular data stream. A Vector Database project is wrong, because time series data streams are not available in Vector Database projects. Metrics with no dimension fields is wrong, because metrics are data point–timestamp pairs identified by dimension fields.

stem: A telemetry store replicates each item on N=3 nodes and must accept a write as long as a single node has durably stored it. According to the Dynamo paper, which setting gives applications that highest level of write availability?
key: `W` set to 1
distractors: `R` set to 1
`W` set to 2
`W` set to 3
explanation: Applications that need the highest level of availability can set `W` to 1, which ensures that a write is accepted as long as a single node has durably written the key. `R` set to 1 is wrong, because `W` is the minimum number of nodes that must participate in a successful write operation, not `R`. `W` set to 2 and `W` set to 3 are wrong, because only `W` set to 1 ensures that a write is accepted as long as a single node has durably written the key.

stem: A Kafka broker serves consumers from the pagecache, and `sendfile` avoids copies through user space. With SSL enabled on the listener, the broker does not use `sendfile`. According to the Kafka design documentation, what is the reason?
key: TLS/SSL libraries operate in user space, and in-kernel `SSL_sendfile` is not supported by Kafka
distractors: `sendfile` can transfer data only between files, never from pagecache to a socket
Encrypted data cannot be held in the pagecache, so SSL listeners read it from disk
Batches sent over SSL stay compressed in the log, which `sendfile` cannot transfer
explanation: TLS/SSL libraries operate at the user space and in-kernel `SSL_sendfile` is currently not supported by Kafka, so `sendfile` is not used when SSL is enabled. Files-only transfer is wrong, because modern Unix systems offer an optimized code path for transferring data out of pagecache to a socket, which Linux does with `sendfile`. Disk reads for SSL are wrong, because all disk reads and writes go through the unified OS cache. Compressed batches are wrong, because a batch remains compressed in the log and is transmitted to the consumer in compressed form.
extract: TLS/SSL libraries operate at the user space (in-kernel SSL_sendfile is currently not supported by Kafka).

stem: A telemetry store assigns each node one random position on a consistent-hashing ring. According to the Dynamo paper, what first challenge does the random position assignment of each node create for the basic algorithm?
key: Non-uniform data and load distribution
distractors: Every node must store a copy of every key on the ring
Every arrival or departure of a node forces all other nodes to move data
The output range of the hash function cannot be treated as a ring
explanation: The random position assignment of each node on the ring leads to non-uniform data and load distribution. Storing every key on every node is wrong, because each node is responsible only for the region of the ring between it and its predecessor. Forcing all other nodes to move data is wrong, because departure or arrival of a node only affects its immediate neighbors. An unusable ring is wrong, because the output range of a hash function is treated as a fixed circular space or ring.
